title: Greenfield v. Philles Records, Inc.
lead: The Ronettes’ recordings acquired new commercial uses long after their recording contract, producing a dispute about ownership, royalties, and one singer’s divorce release.

actors.name: The Ronettes
actors.role: Veronica Bennett, later Ronnie Greenfield, Estelle Bennett, and Nedra Talley

actors.name: Philles Records and Phil Spector
actors.role: Recording company and producer defending the ownership grant

proceedings: New York Supreme Court awarded approximately $3 million with interest.
Appellate Division affirmed, permitting industry-rate unjust-enrichment recovery.
Court of Appeals modified and remitted for contractual royalty calculations, otherwise affirming.
limits: Compilation uses and their compensation were not presented on this appeal. The masters predated federal sound-recording copyright protection; the decision interprets this agreement, not all modern copyright transfers. All five participating judges agreed.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent full-opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The Ronettes record for Philles
sections.cue: Ownership and compensation enter the same contract
paragraphs: Veronica Bennett, later Ronnie Greenfield, her sister Estelle Bennett, and their cousin Nedra Talley formed the Ronettes in the early 1960s. In 1963 they met producer Phil Spector and signed a five-year personal-services agreement with his company, Philles Records. They promised to record exclusively for Philles, which acquired the recordings and agreed to a royalty schedule. Without counsel, they accepted a collective advance of about $15,000.

The group recorded dozens of songs, including the million-selling “Be My Baby,” before disbanding in 1967. Its recording exclusivity did not prohibit income from concerts, television or movie appearances, or reproduction rights to those performances. Philles eventually ceased business. Apart from the advance, the artists received no royalties.

The contract’s introductory language contemplated phonograph records, tape recordings, and similar devices, excluding radio-broadcast transcriptions. Its operative clause made the recordings, reproductions, and embodied performances entirely Philles’ property, free of the artists’ claims. It permitted reproduction through methods then known or later developed, sale under chosen labels, or no exploitation at all.

sections.title: New markets revive the recordings
sections.cue: The singers sue over uses and unpaid royalties
paragraphs: Greenfield married Spector in 1968. Their 1974 California divorce settlement contained mutual general releases addressing past and future claims involving them and Spector’s companies.

Later, renewed interest in 1960s music and new technology increased the value of the old recordings. Defendants licensed synchronization with films and television, including “Be My Baby” in the 1987 film Dirty Dancing. They also licensed third parties to produce and distribute domestic audio recordings and sold compilation albums. They earned substantial compensation but paid the artists no royalties.

The artists sued in 1987, challenging synchronization and domestic third-party licensing and seeking compilation royalties. Defendants first denied a contract existed, but in 1992 stipulated that an unexecuted copy would govern. They then defended the uses under its ownership grant, subject to its compensation obligations.

After extensive proceedings, New York Supreme Court awarded roughly $3 million in damages and interest. The Appellate Division affirmed and permitted unjust-enrichment recovery at an industry-standard royalty of 50% for synchronization and third-party licensing. The Court of Appeals granted leave; compilation authorization and compensation were not issues on that appeal.

sections.title: Unconditional ownership encompasses the disputed uses
sections.cue: The Court of Appeals separates silence from ambiguity
paragraphs: The artists conceded that Philles received unconditional ownership of the masters but argued that the failure to name synchronization or domestic third-party licensing reserved those uses or made the agreement ambiguous. Judge Graffeo, writing for all five participating judges, rejected that interpretation. Under New York law a complete, clear writing supplies the best evidence of intent; ambiguity is a legal question, and outside evidence cannot rewrite definite language to produce a fairer bargain. These masters predated federal statutory copyright protection for sound recordings in 1971, so the court addressed the common-law contract transfer before it.

The court compared Pushman’s outright painting sale, Burnett’s broad assignment of play rights permitting a Casablanca television spinoff, and Boosey & Hawkes’ broad Fantasia music license encompassing later videocassette and laser-disc distribution. Those decisions supported requiring an express reservation when the grant was comprehensive. They did not mean every limited license conveys every right. Warner Bros. v. Columbia Broadcasting’s grant of only specified aspects of The Maltese Falcon illustrated that different situation.

Read as a whole, this contract’s reference to similar devices fit the express permission for future reproduction technologies and did not narrow full ownership. Its royalty schedule regulated compensation, not the uses Philles could authorize. The court distinguished Thomas v. Gusto Records’ royalty question and rejected its suggestion that silence concerning a royalty category itself creates ambiguity. It also directed that Caldwell v. ABKCO’s reliance on that proposed reservation rule not be followed. Although the result excluded the Ronettes from synchronization profits under this bargain, sympathy could not supply a retained right.

sections.title: Payment and the divorce release survive distinct inquiries
sections.cue: A modified judgment returns for recalculation
paragraphs: Philles’ authority to license the recordings did not erase promised royalties. Defendants conceded that the domestic-sales schedule covered audio reproductions, including records and compact discs, sold by their domestic licensees. Those sales required compensation under the contract, not the substituted 50% industry rate.

Defendants also invoked Greenfield’s divorce release. California law governed that California instrument and divorce. Unlike New York’s four-corners approach to the recording contract, California permitted preliminary consideration of credible evidence supporting a meaning the release could reasonably bear, as explained in Pacific Gas & Electric. Supreme Court found that compensation under the 1963 agreement was not an intended subject of the release, and the Appellate Division affirmed. The Court of Appeals left that supported finding intact, allowing Greenfield to participate in properly assessed damages.

On October 17, 2002, the Court of Appeals modified the order without costs and remitted the case to Supreme Court to calculate royalties consistently with the contract, otherwise affirming. Judges Levine, Ciparick, Wesley, and Rosenblatt joined Graffeo; Chief Judge Kaye and Judge Smith did not participate. The approximately $3 million award was neither simply affirmed nor replaced with dismissal of the artists’ entire action.
